title: Chapter 19: Relational Databases, SQL, and JDBC
description: Design durable relational state and access it safely from Java. Learners normalize a schema with keys and constraints, write joins and aggregates, read query plans and index tradeoffs, evolve schemas through migrations, bind values with PreparedStatement, manage pooled connection ownership, and test commits, rollbacks, isolation anomalies, locking, and deadlock recovery.

lessons.title: Tables, keys, constraints, relationships, and normalization
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Tables, keys, constraints, relationships, and normalization

## Relational structure encodes rules
```sql
CREATE TABLE task (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  CHECK (status IN ('OPEN', 'DONE'))
);
```
The SQL dialect may require adjustments in an external database lab. A primary key identifies each row; a foreign key references another table; UNIQUE prevents duplicates; NOT NULL and CHECK constrain values. Application validation improves feedback, while database constraints protect all writers.

## Normalization
Storing a customer's address repeatedly on current orders creates update anomalies if all copies must change together. Separate facts according to their dependencies. Historical order-address snapshots may intentionally remain separate because they represent what was true at purchase time. Normalization is about meaning, not splitting every field into another table.

## Practice
Model tasks, users, assignments, and tags, including a many-to-many link table. Choose deletion behavior for referenced users. Insert duplicate keys and invalid statuses to observe constraints. Explain why a Java check followed by insert cannot alone prevent concurrent duplicate creation.

exercises.title: Tables, keys, constraints, relationships, and normalization: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why retain a database unique constraint after application validation?
choices: Concurrent writers can race past application checks
hints: Picture two requests passing an application-level uniqueness check at the same instant, then ask what stops both from inserting.

lessons.title: SELECT, joins, grouping, indexes, and query plans
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# SELECT, joins, grouping, indexes, and query plans

## Query logical stages
```sql
SELECT u.id, COUNT(t.id) AS open_count
FROM app_user u
LEFT JOIN task t ON t.owner_id = u.id AND t.status = 'OPEN'
GROUP BY u.id
ORDER BY u.id;
```
The LEFT JOIN keeps users without open tasks. Moving the status condition into WHERE can eliminate unmatched rows and change the result. COUNT(t.id) counts non-null matched IDs; COUNT(*) would also count the retained unmatched row.

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups. ORDER BY is required for contractual result order. Pagination needs a stable ordering and a strategy for concurrent changes; offsets can become expensive at scale.

## Indexes and plans
An index accelerates supported access paths while adding storage and write work. Column order and selectivity matter for composite indexes. Read EXPLAIN output against representative data rather than assuming an index is used.

## Practice
Seed users with zero, one, and several tasks. Compare inner and left joins. Add an index for owner/status queries and inspect the plan before and after. Explain why selecting every column can increase I/O and coupling.

exercises.title: SELECT, joins, grouping, indexes, and query plans: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: How can a WHERE condition on the right table change a LEFT JOIN?
choices: It has no effect on join results
It can remove the unmatched rows
hints: Trace whether the filter runs during the join (in the ON clause) or after it (in WHERE), and what happens to an unmatched row's null columns in each case.

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, affected rows, and schema evolution
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, affected rows, and schema evolution

## Every modification needs a target
```sql
UPDATE task SET status = 'DONE'
WHERE id = 42 AND status = 'OPEN';
```
The condition includes the expected prior state. An affected-row count of zero may mean absence or a conflicting state; define how the application distinguishes them. Forgetting WHERE can update every row. Verify destructive statements in a disposable test database.

INSERT supplies rows subject to constraints. DELETE removes rows and may trigger foreign-key restrictions or cascades. Upsert syntax and behavior vary by database; do not assume one dialect's statement is portable.

## Evolve schemas safely
Version migrations and test against a previous populated schema. Adding a non-null column to existing data requires a backfill/default strategy. For rolling deployments, add compatible structures first, migrate data, switch readers/writers, and remove old structures only after old code is gone.

## Practice
Create and complete a task while checking row counts. Attempt a forbidden delete under a foreign key. Write a migration adding priority and test old rows receive a meaningful value. Include recovery and backup assumptions; automatically dropping data is not a safe rollback plan.

exercises.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, affected rows, and schema evolution: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why check an update's affected-row count?
choices: The expected row or prior state may not exist
hints: An UPDATE's WHERE clause encodes an expected prior state; consider what a zero-row result tells you versus a one-row result.

lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 19 assessment

Apply this chapter's schema, transaction, and JDBC reasoning to the decision scenario, then repair **SQL NULL is not the string NULL** with the same attention to constraints and query semantics the joins, updates, and prepared-statement lessons modeled. Write a prediction for what the broken SQL predicate will produce before running the debugger, and preserve the intended query semantics when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

choices: A database constraint with defined conflict handling

exercises.title: Chapter 19 implementation lab: placeholders
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `placeholders`. Return count comma-separated question marks; non-positive counts produce an empty string. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Counts are at most 10000; nonpositive inputs return empty text. This helper does not validate SQL execution: complete the JDBC external lab separately.
hints: Build the count question marks and join them with commas, without a leading or trailing separator.
Return an empty string for zero or negative counts before attempting to build any placeholders.

exercises.title: SQL NULL is not the string NULL
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `SELECT id FROM task WHERE owner_id IS NULL`. The query currently compares owner_id to NULL with `=`, which SQL never evaluates as true; preserve the surrounding string construction while correcting the null predicate, and explain why your fix changes the result instead of hard-coding the print. Output tests verify the printed result; preserving the intended query semantics requires reading the source, not just matching output.

tests.expected: SELECT id FROM task WHERE owner_id IS NULL

hints: Use SQL's null predicate, not equality.
